subject: hadith
summary: Jami' al-Tirmidhi is one of the six canonical hadith collections (Kutub al-Sittah), compiled by Imam Muhammad ibn Isa al-Tirmidhi (209–279 AH / 824–892 CE). It is distinctive among the Kutub al-Sittah for its explicit grading of narrations and its encyclopaedic presentation of scholarly disagreement on each legal point, making it one of the most pedagogically valuable hadith works ever produced.
overview:
Imam Abu Isa Muhammad ibn Isa al-Tirmidhi was born in Tirmidh (present-day Termez, Uzbekistan) around 209 AH and died there in 279 AH. He was among the most prominent students of Imam al-Bukhari and also studied under Abu Dawud, Yahya ibn Ma'in, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. He is reported to have gone blind in his later years, yet continued to teach from memory.

The Jami' al-Tirmidhi is commonly referred to as al-Sunan, though its more accurate title is al-Jami' al-Kabir, reflecting its broader scope beyond purely legal narrations: it covers tafsir, aqeedah, manners (adab), zuhd (asceticism), and the virtues of various acts, in addition to jurisprudential topics. Its structure broadly follows the standard fiqhi order but is supplemented by sections absent from the more strictly legal collections.

Al-Tirmidhi's most significant methodological contribution is his explicit grading system applied to virtually every hadith in the work. He used categories including: sahih (sound), hasan (good), da'if (weak), gharib (strange, with only one chain), and combinations such as hasan sahih or hasan gharib. His category of hasan was in many respects an innovation in hadith terminology, and his use of it remains the subject of scholarly analysis. By grading each hadith, al-Tirmidhi made his collection a self-contained tool for assessing evidential weight.

Equally notable is his practice of summarising the positions of different schools of fiqh after each hadith. Under a hadith on prayer, for instance, he would note: 'This is the position of the Shafi'is; the Hanafis hold such-and-such based on another narration; the Malikis hold this position.' This comparative approach makes the Jami' invaluable for understanding how the same hadith is received differently across the legal schools, and for tracing the textual basis of each school's positions.

The Jami' contains approximately 3,956 hadith. The book concludes with two highly regarded sections: a chapter on al-'ilal (defective narrations) discussing the theoretical principles of hadith criticism, and the Kitab al-Asma' wal-Kunah (a biographical dictionary of narrators). Al-Tirmidhi also authored al-Shama'il al-Muhammadiyyah, a separate work on the physical and moral attributes of the Prophet ﷺ, which has become one of the most beloved texts in the Islamic tradition.

The standard commentary is Tuhfat al-Ahwadhi by Imam Muhammad Abd al-Rahman al-Mubarakfuri (d. 1353 AH), a comprehensive ten-volume work that explains vocabulary, discusses isnads, and analyses scholarly disagreements. Earlier commentaries include Aridat al-Ahwadhi by Ibn al-Arabi al-Maliki (d. 543 AH).

The standard Arabic edition is published by Dar al-Gharb al-Islami (Beirut), edited by Bashshar Awwad Maruf, and is considered the most critically edited modern edition. A research edition by Bashshar Awwad Maruf (Dar al-Gharb al-Islami, 6 vols.) provides detailed source notes and narrator evaluations. The English translation is by Abu Khalyl (Darussalam, 2007), published in six volumes.

The Jami' occupies a unique pedagogical role in the Islamic curriculum. Because it presents both the hadith and the scholarly disagreement over each ruling — often noting the positions of as many as four or five scholars or schools — it serves as an introduction to comparative fiqh as much as a hadith collection. Students of Islamic law who wish to understand how the schools derive their positions from prophetic texts find al-Tirmidhi's work an unparalleled guide. The section on zuhd (asceticism and detachment from the world) is particularly beloved and has been studied and taught separately. Al-Tirmidhi's separate work al-Shama'il, cataloguing the appearance, habits, and character of the Prophet ﷺ, has been commented on by Imam al-Nawawi and many others and remains widely read and recited. The Jami' is available in full on sunnah.com.
